title: 3-Read Friday #16: the Knowing-Doing Hump, QLAs, and Product of Primes
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #16 curates three posts on the gap between knowing and doing, data analysis, and curriculum sequencing. Paul Cline uses his own two-year failure to set up a visualiser to explore why teachers often don't act on practices they already know would help, even when motivated to improve. Craig Latimir offers seven practical ways to make Question Level Analyses (QLAs) more useful than the colourful but often superficial spreadsheets they tend to become. Dan Draper takes a deep dive into sequencing the teaching of product of primes, discussing how he structured tasks and resources around the concept. Barton connects the three as a reminder that good intentions, good data, and good sequencing all require deliberate follow-through to translate into classroom impact.
points: Paul Cline's own two-year failure to set up a visualiser illustrates the "knowing-doing gap" -- knowing a practice will help is not sufficient to guarantee a teacher acts on it.

Craig Latimir's QLA advice emphasises returning to the actual question behind a red column, comparing performance to a nationally representative benchmark, and focusing reteaching on the highest-leverage gaps rather than every gap.

Dan Draper's product-of-primes sequence uses variation -- holding some values constant while changing others -- to force students to reason about structural relationships rather than write out expanded forms.

Barton's throughline: whether the obstacle is personal habit, data overload, or curriculum sequencing, good teaching outcomes depend on deliberate, sustained follow-through rather than one-off good intentions.
quotes: This fascinating post from Paul looks at the reasons teachers may not make changes to their practice, even though they know it is the right thing to do.
Paul illustrates the issues through his own desire to use a visulaiser more, which has never materialised into actually using a visualiser more.
I chose this one because I have long had an issue with Question Level Analyses (QLAs): they take ages to fill out, and I am not convinced they have a positive impact on student learning.
Craig is more positive than me, discussing seven ways teachers can use QLAs more effectively.
Dan does exactly this for the product of prime factors, discussing the sequencing of the lessons, together with the quality resources he has assembled.
